e: Borrowed from French roquette. Cognate with rocket, see that entry for other cognates.
Coined 1899 by removing the first and last letters from croquet.
From French roquelaure, from the name of Antoine Gaston de Roquelaure.
q: Putting on a mask of black silk and drawing a roquelaire closely about my person, I suffered him to hurry me to my palazzo.
1846, Edgar Allan Poe, The Cask of Amontillado:
“Oh Miss Thorne, look here!” said she, as soon as she found herself in the drawing-room, ”do look at my roquelaure! It's clean spoilt, and for ever."
1857, Anthony Trollope, Barchester Towers, Volume the Second, →ISBN, page 97:

e: From translingual roqueforti + -ine, after Penicillium roqueforti, from which it was first isolated.
